# In-House Greenhouse - A new generation of smart greenhouses
Sensors (soil moisture, temperature, humidity and water level sensor)

The software behind the physical IoT greenhouse allows it to be managed autonomously. Its software, which has been named "GreenCore," enables the greenhouse to autonomously handle both the configuration part (at the first power-up, a greenhouse must be registered within the system via API). It has been entirely implemented in Java, employing parallel programming techniques to optimize sensor reading processes. Furthermore, the Pi4J library (version 1.4, link) is used to control the GPIO pins of the Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+.

For API communication, it's mandatory to use HTTP POST requests with the GraphQL query contained in the request body. For more information on creating these queries, you can consult the official guide: GraphQL Queries Guide.

The entire system was developed through Apollo Server (link), a suite that combines the well-known back-end framework ExpressJS with the fantastic query language GraphQL. To further facilitate database development, the Prisma ORM (link) is used. This framework allows you to describe the database structure in textual form (a so-called "schema") and, through an operation called "migration," transform it into SQL commands that are executed automatically inside the PostgreSQL server, applying schema changes automatically to the various tables.

- **PII redaction** *(opt-in, off by default)* — when enabled, query tool output passes through a regex-based redactor that rewrites detected PII spans across **46 built-in entity types** spanning seven categories: personal (email), financial (cards, IBAN, UK bank accounts, sort and US ABA routing codes, CVV), government IDs (SSN, ITIN, EIN, UK/US passports, NHS, NINO, SIN, VAT), contact (phone), network (IP, URL, MAC), digital identity (API keys, JWTs, PEM private keys, password hashes), and crypto wallets. Toggle: `DBMCP_PII_ENABLE` (`pii.enabled`). Operator: `DBMCP_PII_OPERATOR` (`pii.operator`) — one of `replace` (default, entity-aware placeholders like `<EMAIL_ADDRESS>`), `mask` (length-preserving `*`), `redact` (drop), `hash` (SHA-256 hex). Optional subset via `DBMCP_PII_CATEGORIES` (`pii.categories`) (comma-separated, e.g. `financial,government`); unset enables all built-ins. Scope: query tool output payloads only. See PII configuration for the full surface.

- **ML/NER redaction** *(opt-in at runtime, off by default)* — adds `PERSON`, `LOCATION`, `ORGANIZATION`, `NATIONALITY_RELIGION_POLITICS`, and `FACILITY` detection that regex cannot catch, enabled via the `DBMCP_PII_NER_ENABLE` (`pii.ner_enabled`) toggle plus a user-supplied model directory. Which entities are produced depends on the model's labels (CoNLL models give person/location/organization; OntoNotes-class models add NRP and facility). Inference uses **ONNX Runtime** (model directory holds `config.json`, `tokenizer.json`, `model.onnx`; recommended: the MIT-licensed `dslim/bert-base-NER` exported to ONNX, int8-quantized for speed). Fail-closed: a model that cannot load aborts startup and an inference error fails the request — never a silent fallback. Respects `pii.categories`. English for v1.

> **Two different programs answer to that name.** Check which one you have before copying a command below. A **source checkout** carries the repo-root `bin/grappa`, a docker-compose wrapper with the full verb table. A **packaged release** carries a much smaller one: `mix release` moves the generated boot script aside and installs the dispatcher from `infra/release/grappa.sh` in its place (the `install_operator_cli/1` step in `mix.exs`), so the ghcr.io image, the `.deb`, the AUR package and a bastille / systemd install all get the **release CLI**. A release ships no Mix, so every `grappa.*` mix task — most of the verbs below — is simply not there, and asking for one gets you the boot script's own `ERROR: Unknown command …`.

**Self-hosting?** `INSTALL.md` is the one-command Docker install — `infra/docker/deploy.sh install` generates every secret, builds, brings up the single grappa container, and waits until `/healthz` is green (`update` and `stop` are the sibling verbs; the old `scripts/quickstart*.sh` still work as shims). It also covers exposing it with TLS (Caddy / nginx / mkcert). The workflow below is the **operator / hot-deploy path** used for the production host.

**Don't want to build?** Every `vX.Y.Z` release also publishes a self-contained, multi-arch image (`linux/amd64` + `linux/arm64`) to **`ghcr.io/vjt/grappa`** (`:<tag>` + `:latest`) — pull it instead of compiling from source. It bundles the ERTS + the cicchetto SPA and boots on its own. A one-liner brings it up on a host with only Docker + `curl` (no clone): `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vjt/grappa-irc/main/infra/docker/get.sh | bash` (append `-s -- update` to update an existing box), or copy `compose.release.yaml` if you would rather not pipe a script into a shell. Those are two **different boxes**, not two ways to drive one, so the compose path updates with its own pair — `docker compose -f compose.release.yaml pull` then `docker compose -f compose.release.yaml up -d` — and the `-s -- update` recipe above does not reach it (it looks for a box it never installed, and the `install` it then recommends builds a second, empty one; `INSTALL.md` has the untangling). Note it is a *release* image: it has **no `Phoenix.CodeReloader`**, so it is not the hot-edit dev environment — the Docker Compose stack above stays the development runtime, and **updates on the image path are always cold** (pull + recreate; the data volume survives). The same release also publishes **`ghcr.io/vjt/grappa-shottino`** on the same tag scheme and the same two arches — the `shottino --ircd` bridge, for reaching grappa from irssi/weechat/hexchat/goguma without a checkout to compile it in. See `INSTALL.md` and `docs/OPERATIONS.md`.

**On Arch Linux?** Two **community-maintained** AUR packages repackage the official release assets — `grappa-bin` (the server, cicchetto bundled) and `shottino-bin` (the terminal client and `--ircd` bridge): `yay -S grappa-bin` / `yay -S shottino-bin`, x86_64 only. They are maintained outside this repo (by vash909), not by the project, so they follow tagged releases at the maintainer's pace. They are the only AUR path today: the source recipe in `infra/packaging/aur/` is not published there.

**Packaging grappa yourself?** `PACKAGING.md` is the contract the release pipeline keeps with downstream packagers: release asset names and URLs, package layout, runtime user and paths, configuration keys, supported platforms, the `SHA256SUMS` file, and how a change to any of it is announced.

**An update that changes the toolchain is always cold.** A release bundles its own Erlang runtime (ERTS) and its OTP and Elixir applications. The `.rpm`, the Arch package and the container image are built with whatever Erlang and Elixir their builder ships, and a jail bundles the toolchain of its latest `pkg upgrade` at its next `mix release`, so an update can move the toolchain with no change in this repo. The running node then refuses to load the new code hot: `POST /admin/reload` answers `409 stale_toolchain`, naming what moved, with or without `--force-hot`, and the update takes a restart (issue 1112). The container image is always updated by recreating it anyway. A `.deb`, `.rpm` or Arch upgrade applies itself to a running service: it reloads the new code in place when it can and restarts the service when it cannot, a toolchain move included, so there is nothing to do after the upgrade (`PACKAGING.md`); on a jail or a systemd host, run the cold deploy.

**When the database migrations run depends on the format (issue 1112).** A hot deploy of a source checkout (jail, systemd host, Docker via `scripts/deploy.sh`) applies the pending migrations inside the reload. A cold deploy of one first checks the migrations while the running service still serves — a migration version claimed by two files refuses the deploy with nothing stopped — then stops the service, migrates, seeds the built-in themes and starts the new code, so old code never runs on the new schema; a migration that fails at that point leaves the service down, and the deploy says so. `infra/docker/deploy.sh update` on the published image (and `get.sh -s -- update`) keeps the same order: the new image checks the migrations while the old container serves, then the old container is removed, the database migrated and seeded, and the new container started. A container started from `compose.release.yaml` or a bare `docker run` migrates in its entrypoint at every boot, before the release starts. A `.deb`, `.rpm` or Arch package migrates in its install scripts when the service is not running; an upgrade of a running service migrates inside the reload, or, when it restarts, in the unit's `ExecStartPre` after the new release has checked its migrations — a refused check leaves the service running and fails the upgrade (`PACKAGING.md`).

"Grappa" is Italian distillate — the direct homologue of Korean *soju*. "Cicchetto" is the small glass of wine served at a Venetian *bàcaro*, parallel to *gamja*. A deliberate riff on soju/gamja. It's also a tribute: **Italian Grappa!** has been the call-sign of the Italian Hackers' Embassy at European hacker camps since 2001. This repository isn't affiliated with the association that carries the name today; it borrows the reference in the spirit it was intended — Italian hackers showing up somewhere with a bottle.
- **2002 — Forking Bahamut for Azzurra IRC** — a 21-year-old forking an IRC server to add IPv6 + SSL because the Italian network he'd fallen for needed it. Why IRC, and why Azzurra.
